title: Basics & architecture
intro: Understand how Playwright controls browsers, the Browser → Context → Page model, and write and run your first test.

steps.title: One API, three browser engines
steps.body:
Playwright is an open-source library from Microsoft for automating browsers. With one API you can drive **Chromium** (Chrome, Edge), **Firefox** and **WebKit** (the engine behind Safari).

In Python you use the `playwright` package, and for tests the **pytest-playwright** plugin.

steps.question: Which browser engines does Playwright support?
steps.explain: Playwright ships its own builds of Chromium, Firefox and WebKit and drives all three with the same code.

steps.title: How it differs from Selenium
steps.body:
Selenium sends commands through a separate driver per browser (chromedriver, geckodriver) using the WebDriver protocol.

Playwright talks to its bundled browsers directly over one connection. That makes it fast, and lets it **wait automatically** for elements to be ready before acting, so you rarely need explicit waits or `time.sleep`.

steps.question: In Selenium you often add explicit waits before clicking. Why do you rarely need them in Playwright?
options: Playwright clicks faster than the page loads
Playwright auto-waits for the element to be ready before acting
Playwright retries the whole test on failure
steps.explain: Actions like click() wait until the element is attached, visible, stable and enabled. This removes most flaky waits.

points: Playwright automates Chromium, Firefox and WebKit with one API.
No separate drivers: Playwright downloads and drives its own browser builds.
Auto-waiting removes most explicit waits and sleeps.
notes.remember: Selenium: driver per browser + manual waits. Playwright: bundled browsers + auto-waiting.

steps.title: Three layers
steps.body:
- **Browser**: one running browser process.
- **BrowserContext**: an isolated session inside it, like a fresh incognito window with its own cookies and storage. Creating one is very fast.
- **Page**: one tab inside a context.

Tests get their isolation from contexts, without restarting the browser.

steps.title: The layers in code
steps.body: This plain script (no pytest yet) uses the **sync API**: each line finishes before the next starts.
steps.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=False)
    context = browser.new_context()
    page = context.new_page()
    page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com")
    print(page.title())  # Swag Labs
    browser.close()

steps.prompt: Order the calls needed to open a web page.
steps.explain: Each layer is created from the one above it: Playwright → browser → context → page.

steps.prompt: Complete the code to launch Firefox and open a tab.
steps.code:
browser = p.___.launch()
context = browser.new_context()
page = context.___()
steps.explain: p.firefox, p.chromium and p.webkit are the three browser types. A tab is created with context.new_page().

steps.question: One test needs an admin and a normal user logged in at the same time. What do you create?
steps.explain: Each context has its own cookies and storage, so two contexts behave like two separate users. Pages in one context share the same login.

points: Browser = process, BrowserContext = isolated session, Page = tab.
Contexts are cheap and isolated: one per test, or one per user.
Pages in the same context share cookies and login.
The sync API runs each line in order; use it with pytest.
notes.code:
browser = p.chromium.launch()
context = browser.new_context()
page = context.new_page()
page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com")

steps.title: The page fixture
steps.body: With **pytest-playwright** you don't create the browser yourself. Ask for the `page` fixture and you get a fresh page in a new context for every test.
steps.code:
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_login(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com")
    page.get_by_placeholder("Username").fill("standard_user")
    page.get_by_placeholder("Password").fill("secret_sauce")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Login").click()
    expect(page).to_have_url("https://www.saucedemo.com/inventory.html")

steps.question: What does each test receive from the `page` fixture?
options: The same page shared by all tests
A fresh page in a new browser context
A page that is already logged in
steps.explain: Every test gets a new context, so cookies and storage never leak between tests.

steps.title: Running tests
steps.body:
By default tests run **headless** (no visible window) in **Chromium**. Useful options:

- `--headed` to watch the browser
- `--slowmo 500` to slow each action by 500 ms
- `--browser firefox` to switch engine

steps.prompt: Run the tests in WebKit with a visible window.
steps.explain: --browser picks the engine (chromium, firefox, webkit) and --headed shows the window.

steps.title: Record actions with codegen
steps.body: `playwright codegen` opens a browser and writes code as you click. Use it to discover good locators quickly, then clean the code up yourself.

steps.title: Write your first test
steps.body: Copy the exercise into `my-work/basics/`. Log in to saucedemo as `standard_user` / `secret_sauce`, then check the URL ends with `inventory.html` and the page title is **Swag Labs**. Run it once headless and once with `--headed`.

points: pytest-playwright gives each test a fresh `page` in a new context.
Default run: headless Chromium. Add --headed, --slowmo, --browser as needed.
`expect(page).to_have_url(...)` waits and retries until the URL matches.
`playwright codegen <url>` records actions; use it to find locators.
notes.code:
import re
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_login(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Login").click()
    expect(page).to_have_url(re.compile("inventory"))
notes.remember: Ask for `page`, act, then `expect`. pytest-playwright handles browser and cleanup.

interview.q: How is Playwright different from Selenium?
interview.a: Playwright drives its own builds of Chromium, Firefox and WebKit directly instead of going through a WebDriver driver per browser. It auto-waits before actions, has web-first assertions that retry, isolates tests with cheap browser contexts, and includes tracing, codegen and network control out of the box.

interview.q: What are Browser, BrowserContext and Page?
interview.a: Browser is the running browser process. A BrowserContext is an isolated session with its own cookies and storage, like an incognito window. A Page is a tab in a context. Tests get isolation from new contexts without restarting the browser.

interview.q: Why are browser contexts useful for testing?
interview.a: They are fast to create and fully isolated, so every test can start clean, and one test can simulate several users at once by using several contexts.
